study.title: Proverbs 25 - Wisdom for government, coexistence and self-control
study.overview: This chapter brings together proverbs attributed to Solomon, copied at the time of Hezekiah, and presents practical wisdom for public and private life. The text deals with the relationship between God and kings, prudence in speaking and acting, of the importance of fidelity, the correct response to conflict, the care of words and, finally, the need for self-control. The whole shows that biblical wisdom is not only intellectual: it shapes the character, justice, coexistence and self-government.

outline.title: Proverbs gathered in the time of Hezekiah; humility before kings
outline.explanation: The first verses introduce this new collection of proverbs of Solomon, gathered by the men of Hezekiah. Then the text contrasts the mystery of God's action with the responsibility of kings to investigate and judge wisely. Immediate application is humility: not seek hasty prominence before authorities, but expect to be honored at the right time.

outline.title: Contendas, timely words and fidelity
outline.explanation: This section guides not to enter into disputes quickly and to preserve confidence. Then, it highlights the value of the word said at the right moment, the wise rebuke received with attention and fidelity of those who serve with loyalty. It also warns against empty promises, against impatience and against hard language; the mild and patient response can overcome even resistance from a leader.

outline.title: Moderation, limits and sensitivity to suffering
outline.explanation: Here are warnings against excesses and exaggerated familiarity, including in the use of good things in life and in the relationship with others. The chapter also condemns the false testimony, shows the danger of trusting someone unfaithful in difficult times and rebukes the insensitivity to a distressed heart. Wisdom knows how to speak and act appropriately to the other's state.

outline.title: Love to the enemy, good news and self-control
outline.explanation: The text sends the hungry and thirsty enemy, trusting that God will reward this gesture. Then it compares the gossip and slander to forces that produce damage and reminds that living with a quarrelsome person is exhausting. The chapter ends with images of refreshment, moral corruption and, finally, the decisive principle: whoever does not rule his own spirit is like a city without walls, vulnerable and unprotected.

study.context: According to the historical note provided, these proverbs were gathered by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah. Notes do not allow to detail more safely. The chapter therefore appears as part of a later collection of Solomon's sayings, organized for practical instruction of the people and, in particular, to guide life under authority and in community.
study.theology: Proverbs 25 presents a biblical view of wisdom as submission to God, prudence in the use of speech and integrity in human relations. God is greater than the human capacity for investigation, and the kings, although exercising authority, also need to seek discernment and justice. The chapter values self-control, moderation, fidelity and meekness, showing that true strength is not in impulsiveness, but in the ability to govern desires, words and reactions. There is also an ethic of love for the enemy, which anticipates the logic of goodness taught in all Scripture. In contrast, lies, slander, falsehood and lack of self-control destroy the person and the community. The final image of the city without walls summarizes the need for inner vigilance: without government over the spirit, life is exposed to chaos.

scholarViews.insight: The collection of Proverbs 25:229:27 was gathered during the reign of Hezekiah by wise men, that is, counselors who preserved and organized these sayings of Solomon.
The verse points out that the glory of God is in hiding certain matters, for his wisdom is profound and not fully penetrable to the human being.
The timely and well-placed word is compared to something precious and beautiful, indicating that wisdom includes knowing how to speak at the right time.

questions: How does my way of speaking reveal that I value wisdom more than the immediate impulse?
In which situations do I need to exercise self-control so as not to become similar to a city without walls?
I am willing to treat with kindness who treats me badly, trusting that the Lord sees and rewards?
study.practice: Practice three concrete attitudes this week: first, avoid getting into discussions quickly and preserving the confidentiality of others; secondly, choose timely and mild words, especially when there is tension; third, exercise self-domind in a specific area of your life - such as emotional reaction, word use, appetite or ambition - remembering that biblical wisdom includes knowing how to contain the spirit. If there is someone in conflict with you, make a gesture of kindness instead of feeding hostility.
study.uncertainty: The notes provided allow us to safely affirm only the organization of the chapter at the time of Hezekiah and some interpretative emphases of the commentators. There are differences of reading in certain proverbs, especially in the verses about the use of figurative, false images present, and the exact sense of 'sustaining high things'; therefore, these expressions were treated prudently, without imposing a single interpretation as definitive.
